info.educationalGoals:
By the end of the course, students will be able to:

  • Perform close literary readings of pre-modern global texts, identifying symbols, motifs, and thematic patterns related to food and the body.
  • Situate literary works within their cultural, historical, and social contexts.
  • Construct clear, well-supported analytical arguments in academic writing.
  • Revise their writing in response to feedback, demonstrating improved clarity, structure, and evidence use.
  • Engage comparatively with texts from different world traditions.
info.description: Introduces ways of comparing early world literatures across time and space. May explore fundamental themes such as love, heroism, or the underworld.
info.title: Early World Literatures

ACADEMIC INTEGRITY: YOUR WORK, YOUR SUCCESS

Cheating, plagiarism, or any other form of academic dishonesty harms your own learning, undermines the efforts of your classmates who pursue their studies honestly, and goes against the core values of the university.

To learn more about the academic disciplinary process and relevant academic supports, visit:

info.courseDetails: This writing-intensive course introduces students to early world literatures through the lens of food, feasting, hospitality, agriculture, and the elite culture. Drawing on pre-modern texts from multiple cultural traditions (West Asia/Middle East, the Mediterranean, East Asia, South Asia, and the Americas), we will examine how literary works use food as a vehicle for exploring power, identity, the sacred, social hierarchy, and human–divine relations. Emphasis is placed on close reading, the analysis of symbols and thematic patterns, and the development of critical reading, analytical writing, and argumentation skills. Students will practice university-level writing through short response papers, a midterm essay, and a revised research based final paper.
